featured.name: Bastion
featured.pitch: Command-line detection engine that evaluates Windows and Linux logs against the full public SigmaHQ ruleset and maps every hit to MITRE ATT&CK.
highlights: Custom Sigma grammar evaluator; the 1 unsupported rule is disclosed in every report.
Blind spots split into out-of-scope, unread-telemetry, and writable gaps.
Terminal, JSON, SARIF, Markdown, and self-contained HTML dashboard output.
details: Command-line detection engine: ingests Windows Sysmon/EVTX and Linux auth/syslog, evaluates them in-process against the full public SigmaHQ ruleset, maps every hit to MITRE ATT&CK.
Custom Sigma grammar evaluator (field modifiers, base64/windash/UTF-16 transforms, `N of` conditions); 2,479 of 2,480 pinned Windows rules evaluable, the 1 unsupported rule disclosed in every report.
Reports honest coverage: 314 of 706 enterprise techniques covered by the pinned ruleset, with blind spots split into out-of-scope, unread-telemetry, and writable gaps.

Outputs terminal table, JSON, SARIF, Markdown, and a self-contained HTML dashboard; ships a hand-written 8-rule local pack for techniques SigmaHQ misses; `bastion bench` measures real detection on labelled captures.

screenshots.caption: HTML dashboard from a Sysmon capture, with blind spots and caveats reported alongside detections.

featured.pitch: NIST SP 800-53 / RMF compliance toolkit: describe a system in YAML, get a categorization, a baseline, a System Security Plan, a host scan, and a control-by-control report.
highlights: Emits OSCAL SSP, POA&M, and assessment-results JSON plus readable Markdown.
20 read-only Linux host checks mapped to controls through a table modeled on DISA CCI.
Never auto-pass: reports what it can technically assess instead of inflating results.
details: NIST SP 800-53 / RMF compliance toolkit: describe a system in YAML, get FIPS-199 categorization, an SP 800-53B baseline, a System Security Plan, a read-only Linux hardening scan, and a control-by-control report.
Emits OSCAL SSP, POA&M, and assessment-results JSON plus human-readable Markdown; 20 read-only host checks mapped to controls through a hand-curated table modeled on DISA CCI.

208 tests at 97% coverage. Companion blog post: "Map and Fortress: Why I Built Castellan."

featured.name: Scriptorium
featured.pitch: Multi-tenant document intelligence platform with hybrid retrieval, a knowledge graph, and a tool-using AI agent that returns grounded, cited answers.
highlights: Four services across three languages; runs end to end on a laptop, local LLM included.
Tenant isolation, RBAC, prompt-injection handling, tool allowlisting, citation validation.
Honest status table separates what runs live from what is authored and validated.
details: Multi-tenant document intelligence platform: hybrid BM25 + vector retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion over OpenSearch, a Neo4j knowledge graph, and a tool-using AI agent that returns grounded, cited answers.

Four services across three languages (NestJS BFF, Flask ingestion and agent, Spring Boot retrieval), Next.js frontend, PostgreSQL / MongoDB / OpenSearch / Neo4j; runs end to end on a laptop via docker compose, including a local LLM (Ollama).

Security: server-side tenant isolation, RBAC, parameterized queries everywhere, prompt-injection handling, tool allowlisting, citation validation; 33 HIGH/CRITICAL plus 8 SAST findings driven to zero with no blanket waivers.

DevSecOps CI: Semgrep, gitleaks, Trivy, CodeQL, Syft SBOM, cosign keyless signing; Pact contract tests, Playwright e2e with axe-core accessibility gate; Kubernetes manifests validated on a real cluster, Terraform validated (Checkov 140 passed, 0 failed).
Honest status table separates what runs live from what is authored and validated. Eval: retrieval recall@5 = 1.0 on a small labeled set (stated as a pipeline proof, not a SOTA claim).

featured.name: Watchtower
featured.pitch: A Windows desktop app and SQL Server database for a small SOC: triage Sigma alerts, run incidents through NIST SP 800-61 phases, and verify a tamper-evident audit log.
featured.context: CS 3320 Files and Database, St. Mary's University, fall 2026

readout.v: edit at row 444 caught · T-SQL and C# agree

highlights: Every data change writes a row to a SHA-256 hash-chained audit log, written by SQL Server triggers.
Two independent verifiers, T-SQL and C#, must agree before the chain is reported intact.
The app role has no table permissions: only stored procedures and eight named views.
details: Audit chain: 9 `TR_<TABLE>_Audit` triggers write one `AUDIT_ENTRY` row per changed row. Each row hashes `Audit_id`, analyst, action, table, key, time, old and new JSON, and `Prev_hash`. IDs are gapless under an exclusive applock. Verification flags any ID gap, any `Prev_hash` mismatch, or any recomputed hash mismatch, and reports the first broken row. `usp_VerifyAuditChain` and `AuditChainVerifier.cs` run inside one SERIALIZABLE transaction.

Honest limits of the chain: the hash is unkeyed, so a sysadmin could rebuild every hash after an edit, truncate the tail, or disable a trigger without detection. Anchoring the chain head externally is listed as remediation, not built.

Least privilege: the app signs in with Windows auth, then `sp_setapprole 'wt_app'`. It is denied writes to `AUDIT_ENTRY` and EXECUTE on the append procedures. The analyst ID is fixed in a read-only `SESSION_CONTEXT`. Every write procedure re-checks role and active status through `usp_Session_Require`. The UI hides controls but is not the enforcement point.

Passwords use PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations, a 16-byte salt and a constant-time compare. Accounts lock for 15 minutes after 5 failures, and unknown emails get the same response as wrong passwords. There is no dynamic SQL anywhere: free text is escaped by `fn_ContainsPattern`, and sort columns are checked against an allow list.

Integration tests cover every CHECK, FK and UNIQUE constraint, wrong-role denial on every write procedure, injection strings in every text filter, and app-role denial of `SELECT * FROM ALERT` and `UPDATE AUDIT_ENTRY`. They also check that both verifiers agree after 1,000 random operations and catch modified and deleted rows. Not built: MFA, idle timeout, an account management screen, or live detection (rules are stored, never executed).

featured.name: Lodestone
featured.pitch: An x86-64 Linux debugger in C built on ptrace: int3 breakpoints, instruction stepping, disassembly, backtraces and strace-style syscall tracing.
highlights: Full ptrace lifecycle: launch, attach, int3 breakpoints, single-step, register and memory read/write, detach.
Capstone disassembly, ELF symbols with PIE load bias, frame-pointer backtraces, syscall tracing.
ASan and UBSan clean, with a browser GUI driven live by the debugger's JSON event stream.
details: Architecture: about 3,300 lines of C11. `include/lodestone.h` holds the central `debugger_t` state, `src/inferior.c` owns the ptrace lifecycle and stop classification, `src/repl.c` dispatches 17 commands, and each feature lives in its own module (`breakpoint.c`, `symbols.c`, `backtrace.c`, `syscall.c`, `capture.c`). Capstone is the only external dependency. ASLR is disabled in the child via `ADDR_NO_RANDOMIZE` for reproducible addresses.

Breakpoints and stepping: `break <symbol>` or `break *<addr>` saves the original byte and writes `0xCC`. On SIGTRAP the debugger rewinds RIP by one and restores the byte; resuming single-steps the original instruction with `PTRACE_SINGLESTEP`, re-plants the int3, then continues. Disassembly reads through a breakpoint shadow so planted int3s never appear. Memory uses `process_vm_readv`, with a `/proc/<pid>/mem` fallback for writes to read-only text.

Symbols, stack and syscalls: ELF `.symtab` and `.dynsym` are parsed directly, with no libelf. PIE load bias comes from `AT_ENTRY` in `/proc/<pid>/auxv`. `backtrace` walks the saved `rbp` chain with prologue sniffing. Syscall tracing uses `PTRACE_SYSCALL` with `PTRACE_O_TRACESYSGOOD` and `PTRACE_GET_SYSCALL_INFO`, and named catchpoints stop the target. Attach uses `PTRACE_SEIZE`; `detach` releases the process without killing it.

Interfaces: a command-line REPL, a JSON event mode that emits one event object per line, and a browser GUI. `gui/server.js` bridges the event stream to the browser over Server-Sent Events, so the GUI shows the same stops, registers, disassembly and syscalls as the terminal. Testing: each milestone has a bash `gate.sh` with assertions, and a milestone is committed only when its gate passes. The `m12` gate rebuilds with `-fsanitize=address,undefined` and runs a full session with zero reports. The GUI has its own milestone gates, which drive headless Chromium through Playwright.

Limits, by design: single-threaded x86-64 Linux targets only. No threads, no hardware watchpoints, no DWARF line or variable info (symbol level only), no remote protocol, and no source-level step over, only `stepi`. Attaching to a process that isn't a child needs `ptrace_scope=0` or `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`.

featured.name: Rampart
featured.pitch: Hardens a fresh Rocky Linux 9 server toward the DISA RHEL 9 STIG with Ansible, proves it with OpenSCAP scans before and after, and exports NIST SP 800-53 evidence as OSCAL.
highlights: 16 Ansible roles, every task tagged with its STIG ID; second run reports changed=0.
Unedited OpenSCAP results before and after; 404 of 428 evaluated rules pass after hardening.
437 rules mapped STIG ID to CCI to 800-53 Rev 5; OSCAL 1.1.3 export validates against NIST's schema.
details: Target and method: one Rocky Linux 9.8 lab VM under QEMU/KVM, scanned with OpenSCAP and SCAP Security Guide 0.1.82 using the DISA RHEL 9 STIG profile. Baseline: 163 pass, 260 fail (38.5%). After `make harden`, a reboot and a re-scan: 404 pass, 24 fail (94.4%). Scan results in `results/` come only from `oscap` and none was edited by hand.

Hardening: 16 roles (ssh, audit, pam, accounts, sysctl, kmods, packages, services, mounts, sudo, crypto with the `FIPS:STIG` policy, logging, network, aide, files, boot). Every task is tagged with its STIG ID and SSG rule name, so `ansible-playbook --tags <rule>` applies a single rule. The second playbook run reports `changed=0`, and SSH access is verified after hardening.

Exceptions: `exceptions.yml` lists 25 rules not remediated in the lab, each with a written justification: partitioning that must be decided at install time, a GRUB password that needs an operator's secret, remote log encryption and DNS that need site infrastructure, and SSG MAC rules that contradict the FIPS crypto policy (FIPS was kept).

Evidence: `tools/gen_mapping.py` maps each rule to STIG ID, CCI (from DISA's RHEL 9 STIG V2R8 XCCDF) and 800-53 Rev 5 control (from DISA's CCI list). 437 of 1,540 rules map; the rest are outside the STIG profile and marked unmapped with that reason. `python -m rampart oscal` emits OSCAL 1.1.3 assessment-results that validate against NIST's schema.

Testing and limits: Molecule converge, idempotence and verify against the VM, pytest for the report and export code, lint in CI. Molecule is not run in CI because the runners have no KVM image. Castellan, the intended consumer of the OSCAL export, has no import command yet, so no import is claimed.

screenshots.caption: Before and after one playbook run, from the unedited OpenSCAP scans.
